title: Ἰατρὸς καὶ νοσῶν
titleEn: The Doctor and the Sick Man
part: The Doctor and the Sick Man (Chambry 134)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 134. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: A doctor was treating a sick man.
sentences.n: θεραπεύω is to wait upon and tend; of a doctor it is the technical word for treating a case. The imperfect gives the treatment as something under way rather than done.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ νοσοῦντος ἀποθανόντος, ἐκεῖνος πρὸς τοὺς ἐκκομίζοντας ἔλεγεν· « Οὗτος ὁ ἄνθρωπος, εἰ οἴνου ἀπείχετο καὶ κλυστῆρσιν ἔχρητο, οὐκ ἂν ἐτεθνήκει. »
sentences.tr: Tou de nosountos apothanontos, ekeinos pros tous ekkomizontas elegen· « Houtos ho anthrōpos, ei oinou apeicheto kai klystērsin echrēto, ouk an etethnēkei. »
sentences.l: But the sick man having died, that one said to those carrying him out: « This man, if he had kept off wine and had used clysters, would not be dead. »
sentences.i: But when the sick man died, the doctor said to the men carrying out the body: « This man, if he had kept off wine and used clysters, would not be dead now. »
sentences.n: Τοῦ νοσοῦντος ἀποθανόντος is a genitive absolute again. οἱ ἐκκομίζοντες are the men bearing the body out to burial. The condition is contrary to fact: εἰ with the imperfect in the protasis, ἄν with the pluperfect ἐτεθνήκει in the apodosis. ἐτεθνήκει belongs to the perfect stem, which for this verb means the state and not the act — 'would not be dead', rather than 'would not have died'. ἀπέχομαι takes the genitive of what one keeps off, χράομαι the dative of what one uses. A κλυστήρ is the syringe for an enema, standard equipment of ancient medicine.

sentences.t: Τῶν δὲ παρόντων ὑπολαβών τις ἔφη· « Ὦ βέλτιστε, οὐκ ἔδει σε ταῦτα νῦν λέγειν, ὅτε μηδὲν ὄφελός ἐστιν, ἀλλὰ τότε παραινεῖν, ὅτε τούτοις χρῆσθαι ἠδύνατο. »
sentences.tr: Tōn de parontōn hypolabōn tis ephē· « Ō beltiste, ouk edei se tauta nyn legein, hote mēden ophelos estin, alla tote parainein, hote toutois chrēsthai ēdynato. »
sentences.l: But one of those present, taking-up-the-word, said: « My good man, you ought not to be saying these things now, when there is no benefit in them, but to be advising them then, when he was able to use them. »
sentences.i: But one of the bystanders took up the word and said: « My good sir, you should not be saying this now, when it is of no use; you should have advised it then, when he could still have used them. »
sentences.n: ὑπολαβών is 'taking up the word', the regular Greek for cutting in with an answer; there is no seizing in it, and its commoner twin ὑποτυχών works the same way. Ὦ βέλτιστε is 'O best of men', courteous on its face and dry underneath. One οὐκ ἔδει governs both present infinitives, λέγειν and παραινεῖν; the past sits in the finite verb, so the sense is 'you ought not to have been saying … but to have been advising'.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι δεῖ τοὺς φίλους ἐν καιρῷ ἀνάγκης τὰς βοηθείας παρέχειν καὶ μὴ μετὰ τῶν πραγμάτων ἀπόγνωσιν κατειρωνεύεσθαι.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti dei tous philous en kairōi anankēs tas boētheias parechein kai mē meta tōn pragmatōn apognōsin kateirōneuesthai.
sentences.l: The fable shows that friends must furnish their help at the moment of need, and not, after the giving-up-for-lost of affairs, mock in irony.
sentences.i: The fable shows that friends must give their help at the moment of need, and not mock in irony once the case has been given up for lost.
sentences.n: μετὰ τῶν πραγμάτων ἀπόγνωσιν puts into one noun what English wants as a clause: 'after the despairing of the matter'. κατειρωνεύομαι is to speak in the manner of the εἴρων, saying the reasonable thing with the mockery underneath it — precisely what the doctor did over the corpse.
